question: Which statement best describes The three propagation phases?
options: Most UI events (click, input, keydown) bubble: a click on a button also triggers click listeners on its parents in order from target upward. Some events (focus, blur, mouseenter) do NOT bubble — use their bubbling counterparts (focusin, focusout, mouseover) when you need delegation. Bubbling is what makes delegation possible.

Calling stopPropagation on the event halts its travel through the remaining phases, so ancestor listeners won't fire. Use it sparingly — it can break delegation and outside-click handlers that rely on bubbling. stopImmediatePropagation additionally prevents other listeners on the SAME element from running.

When an event fires, it travels in three phases: CAPTURE (from the document root down toward the target), TARGET (at the element itself), and BUBBLE (back up from the target to the root). By default listeners run in the bubble phase; pass { capture: true } to run during capture. This path is why an event on a child can be observed on its ancestors.

`event.target` is the deepest element where the event originated (the actual thing clicked). `event.currentTarget` is the element whose listener is currently running (where you called addEventListener). In delegation, currentTarget is the parent and target is the specific child — the distinction is essential to handle the right element.

question: Which statement best describes The delegation pattern?
options: Delegation isn't free in clarity: deep DOMs and non-bubbling events complicate it, and very specific handlers may be simpler attached directly. For a handful of static elements, direct listeners are clearer. Delegate when items are numerous, dynamic, or share behavior.
